If the filtered `status_counts` is empty (e.g. all check-ins have status OK or another status not in the map), `sum(status_counts.values()) == 1` is False, so execution falls through to `get_text_list([])` and returns the plural template with an empty list, producing a nonsensical message like \" check-ins detected\" (or, depending on callers, an empty human_status). There is no guard for the zero-count case, unlike the singular case which indexes `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP[list(status_counts.keys())[0]]` (which would KeyError if the single status were not in the map, though the filter prevents that). Two issues: (1) the queryset has no deterministic ordering, so the order in which occurrences are produced to Kafka is unspecified; (2) more importantly, `create_incident_occurrence` is invoked once per check-in in `previous_checkins`, each time passing the full `previous_checkins` list — meaning N occurrences are produced for N check-ins, each with a distinct `event_id` but identical failure-reason evidence computed from the whole list. This matches the original behavior (the diff shows the same loop existed in `mark_failed_threshold`), so it is a faithful move, but the lack of ordering means occurrence production order (and thus 'received' timestamps / detection ordering downstream) is non-deterministic. findings.title: get_monitor_environment_context computes a modified config but returns the unmodified one
findings.body: The function builds a local `config` copy, replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value, and then returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original, unmodified dict) in the `"config"` key of the context. The `config` local variable is dead code. Consequence: the monitor context sent with the issue occurrence contains the raw schedule_type value (e.g. an enum/int) instead of the display string, so downstream consumers of the occurrence event data see inconsistent/untranslated schedule types. Either return `config` or remove the dead copy/display logic.

findings.title: get_failure_reason can raise KeyError when failed_checkins contains only non-failure statuses
findings.body: The function filters `failed_checkins` to statuses present in `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP` (ERROR/MISSED/TIMEOUT). If the filtered `status_counts` is empty (e.g. all check-ins have status OK or another status not in the map), `sum(status_counts.values()) == 1` is False, so execution falls through to `get_text_list([])` and returns the plural template with an empty list, producing a nonsensical message like " check-ins detected" (or, depending on callers, an empty human_status). There is no guard for the zero-count case, unlike the singular case which indexes `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP[list(status_counts.keys())[0]]` (which would KeyError if the single status were not in the map, though the filter prevents that). Consequence: malformed evidence text in the generated issue occurrence when the input contains no recognized failure statuses.

findings.title: Typo in docstring: 'humam' should be 'human'
findings.body: The docstring for `get_failure_reason` reads 'Builds a humam readible string' — two typos ('humam' → 'human', 'readible' → 'readable'). This text was carried over verbatim from the old `mark_failed.py` location. Low impact but it is user/developer-facing documentation that should be corrected while moving the code.

findings.title: Occurrences are created once per check-in but the DB query ordering is non-deterministic, and the loop re-queries check-ins without ordering
findings.body: When an incident threshold is reached, the code fetches `checkins = MonitorCheckIn.objects.filter(id__in=[...])` with no `order_by`, then iterates and calls `create_incident_occurrence` for each. Two issues: (1) the queryset has no deterministic ordering, so the order in which occurrences are produced to Kafka is unspecified; (2) more importantly, `create_incident_occurrence` is invoked once per check-in in `previous_checkins`, each time passing the full `previous_checkins` list — meaning N occurrences are produced for N check-ins, each with a distinct `event_id` but identical failure-reason evidence computed from the whole list. This matches the original behavior (the diff shows the same loop existed in `mark_failed_threshold`), so it is a faithful move, but the lack of ordering means occurrence production order (and thus 'received' timestamps / detection ordering downstream) is non-deterministic. If the intent is one occurrence per failed check-in, ordering should be made explicit (e.g. `.order_by('date_added')`) for reproducibility and stable downstream processing.

findings.title: get_or_create for the active incident is not atomic against concurrent mark_failed calls
findings.body: `MonitorIncident.objects.get_or_create(monitor_environment=monitor_env, resolving_checkin=None, defaults={...})` is used to obtain/create the single active incident. Under concurrent `mark_failed` invocations for the same monitor environment (possible since `mark_failed` only guards the `MonitorEnvironment` row update with a `last_checkin__lte` filter, after which `try_incident_threshold` re-reads `monitor_env.status` from the possibly stale in-memory object), two workers can both observe `status in [OK, ACTIVE]` and both call `get_or_create`. Without a unique constraint on (monitor_environment, resolving_checkin IS NULL) or a transaction/lock, this can create duplicate active incidents or race on `monitor_env.save(update_fields=('status',))`. The original code had the same shape, so this is a pre-existing risk surfaced by the move, but the refactor is a good point to note it; at minimum the status check-and-set is not atomic (read of `monitor_env.status` then later `save` is a TOCTOU window).

findings.title: Public functions moved out of mark_failed.py without re-export; any external importers of mark_failed_threshold / create_issue_platform_occurrence / get_failure_reason / get_monitor_environment_context / SimpleCheckIn will break
findings.body: The refactor deletes `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP`, `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP`, and the `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict from `src/sentry/monitors/logic/mark_failed.py` and moves them to `incidents.py` / `incident_occurrence.py` / `types.py` under new names (`try_incident_threshold`, `create_incident_occurrence`). `mark_failed.py` no longer re-exports them. Any code (including tests, tasks, or other modules) that imports these symbols from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` will now fail with ImportError. The PR description says this is preparation for further work, but as it stands this is a breaking change to the module's public surface; either update all importers in the same PR or add backwards-compatible re-exports.
